To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

co-sintering of proton conducting electrolytes on metal supports is not feasible with most candidate oxides due to phase decomposition, contamination with Si and Cr, or insufficient electrolyte sinterability, but is possible with rare-earth ortho-Niobate electrolyte.

co-sintering of metal-supported protonic oxide electrolytes is a viable fabrication approach for metal supported cells, but requires a careful material selection and processing conditions to avoid electrolyte phase decomposition, evaporation, and contamination with metal support.

the fabrication of proton-conducting electrolyte-supported solid oxide cells via co-sintering is challenging, but the challenges can be addressed and the viability of this approach can be demonstrated.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of metal-supported SOFCs with proton conducting electrolyte materials.
the synthesis of proton-conducting oxides and fabrication of metal-supported solid-oxide cells with these materials by co-sintered approach.
the fabrication of metal-supported solid-oxide fuel cells with a proton-conducting electrolyte.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
co-sintering is a promising fabrication approach for metal supported proton-conducting SOCs.
co-sintering is not the best fabrication approach for metal supported proton conducting cells, and other fabrication methods should be considered for this application.
metal-supported proton-conductive solid oxide fuel cells (M-PSOFCs) can be fabricated by co-sintered processing, but the challenges are substantial and the opportunities are limited.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
co-sintering is a promising fabrication approach for metal supported cells, but it requires a careful selection of electrolyte materials and processing parameters.
the co-sintering approach is a viable fabrication route for proton conducting MS-SOCs with La0.95Ca0.
the co-sintering approach is viable for metal-supported cells using La0.99 Ca0.01Nb0.4 electrolyte and the fabrication of a cell with a total resistance of 50 Ω/cm2 at 600°C.
The main takeaway from our work is that
La1−xCaxNbO4 is the only candidate material with the potential to be developed into a metal-supported proton-conductive solid oxide fuel cell.
the electrolyte materials must be carefully selected to be compatible with the fabrication approach, which is a critical aspect for the successful development of MS-SOC technology.
co-sintering is a viable fabrication approach for metal supported proton conducting solid oxide cell, and the electrolyte material La0.99Nb0.01O4 has high potential for this application.
